title: A rule for life
hook: after five years, a lasting rule: small, steady, yours
tomorrow: morning or night: when does prayer actually stick?

segments.voice: The last block closed on wounds that shine. Five years have been gathering pieces. Now the last climb begins, and it starts with something small: a rule.

Resolutions have a short shelf life: the gym pass, the journal with three entries, the app streak that broke on a Tuesday. Usually it isn't willpower that's missing. It's a shape. Here's an odd detail from someone who built something that lasted. Saint Benedict wrote a rule that Benedictine monasteries still live by. Near the end of it, he calls it a little rule written for beginners. Why would its author call it that?
screen: `RESOLUTIONS DON'T LAST.` → `BENEDICT'S RULE.` → `A LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS?`

segments.voice: Because a rule of life isn't a finish line. It's a trellis, something to grow on. In his prologue, Benedict says he hopes to set down nothing harsh and nothing burdensome. A rule is what you do on ordinary days, so the hard days have something to stand on. Most of Benedict's rule is ordinary: when to pray, when to eat, when to sleep, how to treat a guest. One chapter says every guest should be welcomed as Christ. And the Church's first rule was tiny. Acts says the first believers "were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." Teaching, bread, prayer, together. A rule in one sentence. So how do you write yours after five years? Not by copying a saint's schedule. Start with what already works: the prayer you actually say, the Mass you actually go to, the friend you actually call. Benedict built on what people could keep. Over the next days this block takes the pieces one at a time: daily prayer, Sunday, confession, scripture, service. Today is only the inventory. Small, steady, yours.
screen: `NOT A FINISH LINE: A TRELLIS.` · `NOTHING HARSH, NOTHING BURDENSOME.` · `TEACHING, BREAD, PRAYER.` · `START WITH THE INVENTORY.` · then, large: `WHAT WORKS.`

segments.voice: Find a scrap of paper and write down three things that already hold you up: a prayer, a habit, a person, a place. Don't add anything new yet. Look at the list until the bell, and notice how much is already there. Leave it where you'll see it.
A rule for life. A small, steady pattern of prayer and practice, built on what already works.
The line to keep: what works, the place to build from instead of scratch. See you tomorrow.
